parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a company to report a fault with a new washing machine.
script: Good afternoon, Brightwave Appliances customer care, Tamsin speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hello. I'm calling about a washing machine I bought from your website last month. It's only been in the house for three weeks and it's already giving me trouble.
I'm very sorry to hear that. Let me take a few details first, and then we'll see what we can do. Could I have your surname, please?
Thank you, Mr Zielinski. And is there a number we can reach you on during the day?
My mobile's best. It's 07700 912 468. Please don't use the landline, because I'm never there.
Lovely. Now, could you give me the model number? It should be on a silver sticker, either on the back or inside the door.
Hold on, let me have a look. It's tucked away behind the drum, so I need my torch. Right, I've got it. The name is Aquapro, and the number underneath says W-M 4471.
W-M 4471, thank you. Now, I have an order date of the ninth, but that isn't the same as the day it arrived. When was it actually delivered?
Well, I ordered it on a Friday, but the delivery men didn't turn up until the following Tuesday. So it's been three weeks since that Tuesday.
Right, so delivered on a Tuesday. That's well within the guarantee, anyway. So what exactly is the problem?

Water. There's a puddle on the kitchen floor every time I use it. At first I thought the hose at the back had come loose, so I tightened it, but that made no difference. In fact the water is coming from the door, along the bottom edge.
I see, so it's leaking from the door. Is there anything showing on the display when that happens?
Yes, it flashes a code and then the machine stops. E42, I think. No, hang on, I've got that the wrong way round. It's E24.
E24. That's the code that tells us the door seal isn't closing properly. Does it happen with every wash?
No, not every one. The quick wash is fine, and so is the delicates programme. It only leaks when I put the cotton programme on, the really hot one.

That's very useful. I'll note that it only happens on the cotton programme. Now, I'd like to send an engineer to take a look. We could try for tomorrow, Thursday, but I'm afraid every slot is already taken. The next available day is Friday.
Friday would be fine, as long as it's the morning. I work from home on Fridays, but I have to go out in the afternoon.
Morning it is. The engineer will aim to arrive between 8 and 12. He's usually good about phoning ahead. Shall I ask him to call you half an hour before he comes?
Half an hour is a bit long. 20 minutes will do. I'll probably be in the garden, and it only takes me a couple of minutes to come in.
That's fine, I'll put it in the notes. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
Just the cost. I won't be charged for the visit, will I?

Not at all, it's covered by the guarantee, so there's nothing to pay for the visit, the parts or the labour. If the engineer needs to order a new part, he'll tell you on the day and fit it as soon as it arrives. Now, I'll give you a case reference in case you need to ring us again. It's R-B 5530. Have you got that?
R-B 5530. Yes, I've written it down. Thank you very much for your help.
You're welcome, Mr Zielinski. I hope the machine is working properly again soon. Have a good afternoon.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A site manager briefs staff on the morning of an outdoor music festival.
script: Right, everyone, if you could gather round, because I'd like to get through this before the sound check starts at half past ten. Welcome to the briefing for today's Tilbury Fields Music Day. For anyone who hasn't worked with us before, I'm Greg Pascoe, the site manager, and I'll be on the radio all day if you need me.

First, the basics. The gates open to the public at 12, but you needed to be here much earlier, and I'm glad to see you all made it. Now, when you arrived, I hope nobody went to the main gate to collect their wristband and radio. That queue gets chaotic, so everything is handed out in the staff tent. That's the white one behind the main stage. If you haven't picked up your radio yet, go there as soon as we finish and Sandra will sort you out.

Next, what's different this year. We've sold nearly 6,000 tickets, which is a record, and we've changed the way people pay. Last year we took cash at every stall and it caused long queues, so this year every stall and the bar take cards and phones only. There is no cash on site at all. There are two cash machines outside the gates if anyone asks you. I know a few people have been asking whether we've added a second stage. We haven't. It's the same single stage as before, and we still finish at half past ten.

Now, radios. Please learn the channels, because it matters. Channel 1 is for emergencies only, that means security and first aid. Channel 3 is kept for the artists' team. Everything else, such as asking for more bins, or a break, or a bag of ice, goes on channel 2. If you're not sure which channel to use, listen first, and wait for a gap before you speak.

One more thing before I give you your positions. If you find a child who seems to be lost, please don't carry them off to the first aid tent, because that's for medical problems only, and don't set off around the site looking for the parents. Stay exactly where you are, keep the child with you, and radio the information point. Someone will come to you within a couple of minutes. The child will be much calmer if you stay in one place.

Right, here's where everyone will be. Jo, you did the main gate last year, so this time I'm putting you in the car park. The first cars arrive at about 11, so you'll have a long day, but there's a flask of tea waiting for you in the tent.
That means Karim takes over at the main gate. You'll be working with two volunteers, and your job is to check tickets and to give out the programmes.

Lena, you're in the food court. Please make sure every stall has its hygiene certificate on display and that the queues don't block the path to the toilets. I know it looks easy, but it gets very busy at about two, when the first band finishes.

Pete, I'd like you on the recycling points. There are three of them, one by the stage, one in the food court and one at the bar. Please don't just empty the bins. Stand beside them and talk to people about what goes where. It's much more effective than a sign.
Sunita, you're our qualified first aider, so you'll be in the first aid tent, right next to the staff tent. There will be a paramedic with you, and you'll have the radio on channel 1 at all times.

And finally, Wei. I'd originally put you on the artists' area, but Dina has asked to do that herself, so you're in the camping field. It doesn't open until 3, but you'll be on duty until midnight, and I'm afraid there's no getting out of it. We need someone there who can deal with noise complaints calmly.

That's everybody. If you aren't sure about your position, have a look at the plan pinned inside the tent. Remember to drink plenty of water, because it's going to be hot, and please wear your high-visibility jackets at all times. Any questions? No? Good. Then let's have a great day. Thanks, everyone.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A geography student asks her tutor for advice about choosing an optional module for her second year.
script: Come in, Marisol, and take a seat. You said in your email that you wanted some advice about next year.
Yes, thank you for seeing me. I have to choose one optional module for my second year, and I just can't decide between Coastal Processes and Geographic Information Systems. Everyone calls it GIS.
Ah, the classic dilemma. Tell me what's pulling you towards each of them.

Well, I loved the beach fieldwork we did in the first year, when we measured the slopes at Sandwick. But my sister works for an engineering firm, and she says employers keep asking for mapping skills, and I've never touched that kind of software.
Both are sound choices. Is there anything about Coastal Processes that worries you?
Honestly, it's the residential field trip. Last year's students told me it was ten days in Wales and cost nearly 600 pounds. I can't afford that.
Ah, that was the old trip. It's now five days, and the department pays for the accommodation, so students only cover their travel. That's around 80 pounds.
Oh, that's a relief. I'd been assuming it was out of the question. I'm not worried about the maths, by the way. I did well in the statistics module.
Good. And what about the way the module is assessed? Some people are put off by that.
I'm much better at coursework than exams, so I hope there's not a big exam.
There is one, a two-hour paper, but it's only worth 40 per cent. The other 60 per cent comes from your field report, so it suits you.
That's good. What about GIS? I think it's taught in the computer labs, isn't it?

That's right, and you don't need any programming experience, because they teach everything from scratch. The one thing I'd warn you about is places. The lab only holds 40 students, and the module fills up very quickly, so you shouldn't leave it to the last minute.
I see. And do I have to buy the software? I don't have much money.
No, it's free for students. You can install it on your own laptop, so you don't have to rely on the lab computers.
Great. So how should I actually decide? Which one do employers like more?

Honestly, they value both. Your sister is right that mapping skills are in demand, but a good field report shows you can collect and analyse your own data. My advice is to pick the one you'll enjoy most, because you'll work harder at it, and your marks will show that.
That makes sense. I think what I need is to see what GIS is really like.

Then why don't you sit in on a practical session? There's one on Tuesday at two o'clock. The Monday lecture is only theory, so I wouldn't bother with that. Just email Dr Penhaligon, who runs the module. That's P-E-N-H-A-L-I-G-O-N. She'll be happy to let you in.
I'll do that this evening. And when do I have to hand in my choice? I thought it was the end of the month.
It was, but the department has brought it forward. The form has to be in by the 24th. You can submit it online, so there's no need to come to the office.
The 24th, right. Thanks. And whichever one I choose, can I still pick up some of the other skills?

Certainly. The Geography Society runs a mapping workshop on Thursday evenings, and it's open to everyone. And if you go for GIS and miss the fieldwork, there's a summer volunteering scheme with the council's coastal team. It's a good way to see a beach in the real world.
That sounds perfect. I feel much clearer now. Thank you so much.
Not at all. Let me know how the practical goes.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer gives a talk on bird nests and what engineers can learn from them.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about something most of us walk past every day without noticing: the bird's nest. I'm going to argue that a nest is a piece of engineering, and that engineers have a great deal to learn from it.

Let's start with what makes nest building so remarkable. A bird has no blueprint, no tools and no hands. It works with its beak and its feet, and nothing else. And yet it produces a structure that has to be strong, waterproof, warm, and light enough to sit on a thin branch. Think how hard it would be for you to build a shelter if you could only use your mouth and your toes.

Let's begin with the weaver birds, which are famous for their skill with knots. The male village weaver takes long strips of grass or palm leaf and ties them to a branch, not by threading them through each other, as the name might suggest, but by making real knots. He works from the top downwards, building a ring, then a roof, and finally an entrance tunnel that points downwards. If a female inspects the nest and doesn't like it, he pulls it apart and starts again. Some males make dozens of nests in a single season.

Now compare that with the hummingbird, one of the smallest builders. The nest is only the size of an egg cup, but it is made with an extraordinary material. The bird gathers spider silk and wraps it around plant fibres. Silk is sticky, so it holds the structure together, and, even more importantly, it stretches. As the chicks grow, the nest expands with them. The outside is covered with moss and bits of lichen, but that's for camouflage, not for strength. The silk does the real work.

Next, let's look at the largest nests of all. The sociable weaver, a small bird of southern Africa, builds a communal nest that is more like an apartment block. It can weigh up to a tonne, and it may house over a hundred pairs of birds. The roof is made of dry grass, laid in thick layers so that rain runs off, and the chambers beneath are lined with softer material. The most interesting thing is the temperature. Outside, it can fall to 5 degrees at night and rise to 40 in the afternoon, but inside the chambers it stays close to 20 degrees. The structure acts as insulation without any machinery at all.

Of course, not every bird uses plant material. The ovenbird of South America builds its nest from mud. It collects wet mud, mixes in straw and a little animal dung, and shapes it into a dome that looks like an old bread oven. The straw does the job that steel bars do in reinforced concrete, giving the mud strength when it dries. Interestingly, the birds don't need to travel far for the material. They usually find it within a few metres of the nest site. These nests can last for years, and other birds often move in once the owners have left.

Then there are the swiftlets of South-East Asia, which nest on the walls of dark caves. They build with their own saliva, which hardens into a cup in the air. The nests are collected for food in some countries, but what interests scientists is the substance itself. Researchers are studying it as the basis of a new kind of surgical glue that could close wounds without stitches, because it sticks well and the body tolerates it.

So what are engineers actually taking from all this? One research group has built small robots that make a structure by adding material one layer at a time, and checking each layer before adding the next, which is exactly how the ovenbird works. What the robots do not copy is teamwork, because they work alone. The point is the slow, step-by-step way a structure grows.

Finally, I'd like to leave you with a bigger idea. It's tempting to think that a bird must carry a detailed plan of its nest in its head. But experiments suggest otherwise. Each bird follows a small number of simple rules, such as adding material where there is a gap, or pushing a twig into the structure until it holds. Out of these simple behaviours, a surprisingly sophisticated structure appears. That, I think, is the real lesson for engineers: complexity doesn't always need a complicated plan. Thank you. Are there any questions?

passages.title: Cityride Bike Hire: how it works
paras: A  Getting started. To use Cityride, download the app or register at any docking station terminal. You will need a valid email address and a debit or credit card. A refundable deposit of 20 pounds is held on your card for as long as you have an account. Registration takes about three minutes, and you can hire a bike straight away.

B  Unlocking a bike. Choose any bike that shows a green light on the dock, then enter the six-digit code displayed on the screen or scan it with your phone. Please check the tyres and brakes before you ride off. If anything looks wrong, press the red button on the dock and take a different bike. Faulty bikes cannot be reserved.

C  Prices. The first 30 minutes of every journey are free. After that, the charge is 1 pound 50 for each further half hour, up to a daily maximum of 12 pounds. A monthly pass costs 9 pounds and gives you unlimited journeys of up to 45 minutes each. Students can claim a 25 per cent discount by emailing a copy of their student card.

D  Returning your bike. Push the front wheel firmly into any empty dock until you hear a click and the light turns green. Wait for the confirmation message on your phone before you leave. If the light stays red, the dock is faulty and you should try another one. If a station is full, use the app to find the nearest dock with free spaces; you will be given an extra 15 minutes free of charge.

E  If something goes wrong. Report accidents, theft or damage using the Help button in the app, or phone our 24-hour line on 0800 555 0142. A bike left outside a docking station, even briefly, may result in a fee of 25 pounds. If a bike is stolen while in your care, you must report it to the police within 24 hours.

F  Riding safely. Helmets are not supplied, but we strongly advise you to wear one. Lights come on automatically after dark. Bikes are designed for one rider and must not be used to carry passengers. The maximum load for the front basket is 10 kilograms. Cityride bikes must not be taken onto trains.

passages.title: Larchfield Housing Association: repairs at Moorcroft Court
paras: Dear residents of Moorcroft Court,

We are writing to let you know about planned repairs to your building. The work will begin on Monday 6 October and is expected to last eight weeks. It is being carried out by Harcourt Building Services on behalf of Larchfield Housing Association.

What will be done. The main job is to replace the flat roof above the stairwell, which has leaked since last winter. Scaffolding will be put up on the north side of the building during the first week. At the same time, the contractors will repair the cracked paving in the car park and repaint the communal corridors on each floor. The windows will not be replaced during this project; that work is planned for next year.

Working hours. Work will take place between 8 am and 5 pm on weekdays. Noisy work, such as drilling, will not begin before 9 am and will finish at 4 pm. There will be no work at weekends unless there is an emergency.

Access. Residents on the top floor may be asked to let contractors into their flats to check for damp. You will be told in writing at least 48 hours beforehand. If you cannot be at home, a neighbour can let them in with your permission. The lift will stay in use except for two days in week four, when it will be switched off for safety checks.

Parking. About a third of the car park will be fenced off at any one time. Reserved bays cannot be guaranteed, but residents who have a blue badge will keep their existing bay. Other residents may use the public car park on Mill Lane, and Larchfield will pay for parking permits for the duration of the work. Collect your permit from the site office.

Your questions. The site manager, Debbie Tran, will be in the site office, which is the ground-floor meeting room, every Tuesday and Thursday from 10 am to noon. You can also phone the housing office on 01632 960 241.
We apologise for any inconvenience and thank you for your patience.

passages.title: Haverford Foods: hygiene rules for production areas
paras: All staff and visitors must follow these rules whenever they enter the production floor. Failure to do so may lead to disciplinary action.

Before you enter. Report to the changing room at the start of every shift. Store your coat, bag and mobile phone in a locker, because phones are not permitted on the production floor. Put on the white coat and hairnet provided, together with blue overshoes. Anyone with a beard or moustache, however short, must also wear a beard cover.

Hands. Wash your hands for at least 20 seconds using the antibacterial soap, then dry them with paper towels, never with your clothes or a cloth. Wash your hands again after every break, after using the toilet, after touching your face or hair, and after handling waste. Disposable gloves are blue, so that they can be spotted easily if one falls into the product. Change them every hour and whenever they are torn.

Jewellery and personal items. No jewellery may be worn, with the exception of a plain wedding ring. Watches, earrings and visible piercings must be removed before the shift begins. Nail varnish and false nails are not allowed, and nails must be kept short and clean.

Illness. If you have suffered from sickness or diarrhoea, you must not return to work until 48 hours after your last symptoms. Tell your supervisor before the shift if you have a cut or sore. It must be covered with a bright blue waterproof plaster, and your supervisor will check it at the start of each shift and again after each break.
Food and drink. Eating, drinking and chewing gum are allowed only in the canteen. Water may be drunk at the marked drinking points in the corridor outside the production floor.
Spills and waste. Report any spillage to your line leader at once. Do not attempt to clean it yourself. Waste must be placed in the red bins and never left on work surfaces.

passages.title: Moving to a new team: writing a CV for an internal transfer
paras: A  Know what you are applying for. Read the job description carefully and make a note of every skill it asks for. Your CV should show that you meet most of them. If you can, have an informal chat with someone in the new team before you apply; it will help you understand what the job really involves and what the manager is looking for.

B  Do not assume you are known. Colleagues may know you well, but the person who shortlists applicants might never have met you. Write as if for a stranger and give a clear picture of your career so far, including the dates and the jobs you have held. People are often surprised by how little their own organisation knows about what they actually do.

C  Focus on results. Instead of listing your duties, describe what you have achieved. You might have cut waste by 10 per cent, trained three new starters or helped your team to meet a difficult deadline. Use figures wherever you can, because a number is more convincing than a general claim.

D  Show skills that transfer. If you are moving to a very different department, explain which of your skills will be useful there. Reliability, teamwork, working under pressure and learning new systems quickly are valued in nearly every role.

E  Keep it short. Two pages is plenty. Put your most recent job first and give less space to older roles. Leave out anything that is unrelated to the post, such as hobbies and personal interests, unless they show a skill that the job requires.

F  Ask someone to read it. Before you send your CV, ask a friend or a colleague from outside your department to check it. They will notice mistakes, and they will tell you if you have used technical terms or abbreviations that only people in your own area would understand.

G  Tell your manager first. Let your current manager know that you intend to apply. They may be asked for a reference, and they will be much less pleased if they hear about your plans from somebody else.

passages.title: The rise of community-owned shops and pubs
paras: A  Walk through almost any rural district of Britain and you will notice what is missing. The village shop with its post office counter, the pub beside the green: both have been disappearing for decades. Supermarkets, online shopping, rising bills and owners who retire without finding a buyer have all played a part. For a small community, the loss of its last shop or pub is more than an inconvenience. It removes the one place where neighbours bump into each other, where news is exchanged and where a newcomer can be introduced to the rest of the village.

B  Yet over the past fifteen years a quiet counter-movement has grown. Rather than wait for a company to rescue the business, local people have started to buy it themselves. In a typical community venture, residents buy shares, sometimes costing as little as 10 pounds, and every shareholder has a single vote, however many shares they own. The aim is not to make a large profit but to keep the doors open, and any surplus is normally spent on the business or on local causes. Several hundred such shops and pubs are now trading across the country, and the number rises each year.

C  Ashby Dene, a village of about 600 people, shows how it can work. When the owner of the shop retired in 2016, nobody came forward to take it on, and the premises stood empty for a month. A neighbour called a public meeting, which 140 people attended. Over the next six months, the villagers raised 85,000 pounds from 212 shareholders, and the shop reopened inside a converted barn on the edge of the green. 'We were surprised by how quickly people came round to the idea,' says Rosalind Teague, who chairs the management committee. 'Once someone said they would put in 200 pounds, everyone else suddenly felt able to put in something.'

D  Raising the money, however, is only the first hurdle. Community shops depend heavily on volunteers. At Ashby Dene around 60 villagers take turns behind the counter, which allows the shop to open for 70 hours a week with only two paid members of staff. The benefit goes beyond saved wages. Volunteers bring their friends and relatives in as customers, and they notice when an elderly regular has not been in for a few days. Some shops have set up a delivery round for housebound residents, run entirely by volunteers on bicycles.

E  Buying from nearby producers is another strength. Many community shops stock vegetables, eggs and bread from farms and bakeries within a few miles, something a national chain rarely does. A survey of 40 such shops carried out by the Strathmore Rural Trust found that, on average, a quarter of what they sold came from suppliers within ten miles. That means a larger share of every pound spent stays in the local economy, and some producers say that having a reliable outlet nearby has allowed them to keep farming at all.

F  Pubs face different challenges. They occupy larger buildings, so heating and repairs cost more, and they usually need a skilled manager rather than a rota of volunteers. Many community pubs have therefore widened what they offer. The Foxglove Inn, bought by its 330 shareholders four years ago, serves coffee and cake in the morning, hosts a weekly lunch club for pensioners, and keeps a small library in the snug. A corner of the bar doubles as a post office on two afternoons a week. 'Beer alone would not have paid the bills,' admits the landlord, Tariq Varga. 'It's the other things that bring people through the door.'

G  Help is available. Some local councils offer start-up grants, and a national scheme allows a community to ask for a pub or shop to be listed as an 'asset of community value'. If the owner then decides to sell, the villagers are given six months to prepare a bid before the property can go on the open market. The scheme has limits, though. It does not oblige the owner to accept the community's offer, nor does it set a price, so a group can still lose out to a developer who is willing to pay more.

H  Not every venture succeeds. A handful have closed within three years, usually because their founders were too optimistic about sales or because the small group of volunteers who did most of the work became exhausted. Advisers now urge new groups to draw up a realistic business plan before they start fundraising, and to recruit far more helpers than they think they need. Even so, the failure rate among community-owned businesses is much lower than among ordinary small businesses. Supporters add that profit is the wrong way to judge them. A shop that makes only a small surplus, they argue, may still be worth a great deal to a village that would otherwise have nothing.
